Here are the verse-by-verse notes based on all available sources.

---

## Leviticus 9 — Verse-by-Verse Commentary

### Overview of the Chapter

The chapter records the inauguration of the tabernacle sacrificial service. After seven days of consecration (Lev 8), on the eighth day Aaron and his sons formally assume their priestly duties. Aaron offers first for himself (vv. 8–14), then for the people (vv. 15–21), blesses the people (v. 22), and then God answers with fire from His presence consuming the sacrifice (v. 24). Several commentators note this chapter is a complete model of how the divinely-given sacrificial system was to be carried out.

**Sources:** https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-9/ ; https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/expositors/leviticus/9.htm ; https://www.preceptaustin.org/leviticus_9_commentary

---

### v. 1 — *“On the eighth day Moses summoned Aaron and his sons and the elders of Israel.”*

- **The eighth day as “new beginnings.”** David Guzik notes that the entire consecration ceremony lasted more than a week and the call to priesthood came on the eighth day — the day of new beginnings. After seven days of patient fellowship with the LORD in His tabernacle, God was ready to do a new work. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-9/)
- **Not the eighth of the month.** Bush (cited at Precept Austin) clarifies: “Not upon the eighth day of the month, but on the first day after their consecration, which occupied seven days.” All creatures were considered in a state of imperfection for seven days and perfected on the eighth (see Lev 12:2–3; 14:8–10; 15:13–14; 22:27). (https://www.preceptaustin.org/leviticus_9_commentary)
- **Elders = “the bearded ones.”** The Hebrew term for elders literally means “the beards” or “the bearded ones,” associating age with authority and wisdom. The same elders who witnessed the consecration (Lev 8:3) now witness the priests entering active duty. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-9/)
- **Jewish tradition:** According to Talmudic tradition, the preceding week began on the 23rd day of the 12th month, so this eighth day was the 1st day of the 1st month (Nisan), the same day the tabernacle was erected (Ex 40:2, 17). (https://www.preceptaustin.org/leviticus_9_commentary)

---

### v. 2 — *“Take for yourself a young bull for a sin offering and a ram for a burnt offering, both without blemish, and present them before the LORD.”*

- **Even after consecration, sin remained.** Guzik: Aaron and his sons lived an entire week at the tabernacle, yet they still had sin to atone for. “The consecration ceremony did not make Aaron perfect. During the seven days of just sitting in the tabernacle he added more sin to his account that had to be cleared.” God also wanted to show through repetition that animal sacrifices were not complete — only the Messiah’s perfect sacrifice could make an end of sins. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-9/)
- **Connection to the golden calf.** Clarke, Trapp, and ancient Jewish tradition (including the Chaldee Version / Targum) hold that the young bull (literally “a calf, the son of a bull”) was specifically to atone for Aaron’s sin with the golden calf (Exodus 32). Clarke: “This is very probable, as no formal atonement for that transgression had yet been made.” Ellicott confirms this is “so old and universal” an interpretation that it appears in the ancient Chaldee Version of the Pentateuch. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-9/ ; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/leviticus-9.html)
- **The ram for a burnt offering** represented ongoing dedication. Even after the prior week’s special consecration, “the idea of consecration had to be ongoing in the life of Aaron and all of God’s priests.” (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-9/)
- **“Without blemish”** — the animals had to be physically perfect, prefiguring the sinless perfection of Christ, the true offering. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/leviticus_9_commentary)

---

### v. 3 — *“Then speak to the Israelites and say, ‘Take a male goat for a sin offering, a calf and a lamb…’”*

- **The people must bring their own sacrifices.** Gill notes that Moses had no more to do with the people’s sacrifices now that Aaron was high priest; it was incumbent on Aaron to call upon the people to bring the required animals. (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/leviticus/9.htm)
- **The male goat (he-goat) was the usual sin-offering victim.** The Expositor’s Bible Commentary notes rabbinical tradition held it was chosen to counteract Israel’s tendency to worship “shaggy he-goats” (demons), referenced in Lev 17:7. (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/expositors/leviticus/9.htm)
- **Five sacrifices for the people** (sin offering, burnt offering, peace offering, and grain offering) — all of which had been described in Leviticus 1–7. On this eighth day, something new would happen: God would appear. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-9/)

---

### v. 4 — *“an ox and a ram for a peace offering…and a grain offering mixed with oil. For today the LORD will appear to you.”*

- **The peace offering was unique to this occasion.** The Expositor’s Bible Commentary: “Peculiar to this occasion, a peace offering for the nation… evidently intended to signify that now on the basis of the sacrificial worship and the mediation of a consecrated priesthood, Israel was privileged to enter into fellowship with Jehovah.” No separate peace offering was ordered for Aaron and his sons because they would share in the people’s peace offering. (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/expositors/leviticus/9.htm)
- **“The LORD will appear”** — Ellicott: “Prepare and sanctify yourselves with these sacrifices, for the Lord is to manifest himself in an especial manner to signify his approval of the inauguration of Aaron and his family to the priesthood.” (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/leviticus-9.html)
- **The glory (kabod):** Rooker (cited by Guzik) notes the Hebrew word for glory comes from the root *kbd*, denoting “heaviness” or “weightiness,” hence “significance, superior value, distinction, splendour.” (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-9/)

---

### v. 5 — *“So they took what Moses had commanded to the front of the Tent of Meeting, and the whole congregation drew near and stood before the LORD.”*

- **Obedience of all the people.** The people brought exactly what Moses commanded — implicit, corporate obedience. “All the congregation drew near” suggests a massive assembly filling the courtyard. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-9/)
- Precept Austin notes the Septuagint translates “the sons of Israel” (v. 3) as “the elders of Israel,” connecting the representative leadership with the whole congregation. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/leviticus_9_commentary)

---

### v. 6 — *“And Moses said, ‘This is what the LORD has commanded you to do, so that the glory of the LORD may appear to you.’”*

- **Obedience precedes glory.** Guzik: “Everything Aaron did in the previous week prepared him for this moment. This was the end goal of the week of separation and consecration to the LORD — the display of God’s glory.” The promise of the glory appearing was conditional on doing “what the LORD has commanded.” (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-9/)
- **Moses as mediator** gives assurance that these instructions are from God. Precept Austin notes v. 6 and v. 10 both affirm “as the LORD commanded Moses,” giving assurance these were among God’s instructions on the mountain though not explicitly recorded earlier. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/leviticus_9_commentary)

---

### v. 7 — *“Then Moses said to Aaron, ‘Approach the altar and sacrifice your sin offering and your burnt offering to make atonement for yourself and for the people…’”*

- **Aaron had to deal with his own sin first.** Guzik: “Aaron had to first deal with his own sin, and only then he could truly function as a priest, ready to serve others.” G. Campbell Morgan: “He could not be the instrument of mediation between the people and God for worship save as he was brought into right relationship with God.” (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-9/)
- **Typological point — the inadequacy of the Levitical priesthood.** Gill: “A man cannot atone for another until he is pure from all sin; which is a character only to be found in Christ, our great High Priest.” The Levitical priests had to offer first for their own sins, showing the imperfection of that priesthood. Christ, our High Priest, “needed not to do this; see Hebrews 7:27.” (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/leviticus/9.htm)
- **“Make atonement for yourself and for the people”** — Ellicott says the wording “goes far to confirm the ancient interpretation” that this addresses the sin of the golden calf, which Aaron and the people committed together (Exodus 32:35). (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/leviticus-9.html)
- **Dummelow:** Aaron did not approach the altar until called by Moses, “showing that he did not take this honour to himself, but that it was the call of God by Moses: cp. Hebrews 5:4–5.” (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcb/leviticus-9.html)

---

### vv. 8–11 — *Aaron’s sin offering for himself*

- **v. 8 — Aaron slaughtered the calf.** As the sacrificer, Aaron slaughtered the victim himself on the north side of the altar (Lev 1:11). This was a public display of honesty and humility — “I am a sinner who needs atonement also.” (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-9/)
- **v. 9 — Blood on the horns of the altar.** Aaron’s sons caught the blood in a bowl and brought it to him. Unlike the normal law for a high priest’s sin offering (where blood was taken into the tabernacle — Lev 4:7), Aaron applied it only to the horns of the bronze altar because he had not yet gained access to the holy place. He poured the rest at the base of the altar — exactly as Moses had done during the consecration sin offering (Lev 8:15). (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/leviticus-9.html)
- **v. 10 — Fat, kidneys, and lobe of the liver.** These were burned on the altar “as the LORD had commanded Moses.” The fat portions belonged exclusively to God. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-9/)
- **v. 11 — Flesh and hide burned outside the camp.** This conforms to the law for the priest’s sin offering (Lev 4:11–12). The Expositor’s Bible Commentary and Hebrews 13:11–13 see this as typifying Christ who “suffered outside the gate.” (https://www.preceptaustin.org/leviticus_9_commentary)

---

### vv. 12–14 — *Aaron’s burnt offering*

- **v. 12 — Aaron slaughtered the burnt offering; blood sprinkled on all sides.** The burnt-offering ritual followed the pattern of Leviticus 1. The blood was “splattered” (or “sprinkled”) around all sides of the altar. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-9/)
- **v. 13 — Piece by piece, including the head.** Peake’s Commentary notes the phrase “piece by piece” suggests “the leisurely solemnity of the whole rite.” Nothing was rushed. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/pfc/leviticus-9.html)
- **v. 14 — Entrails and legs washed and burned.** The washing of the inward parts and legs symbolized inner purity before being offered to God. Everything was burned — the burnt offering was wholly consumed, representing total dedication. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-9/)

---

### v. 15 — *“Aaron then presented the people’s offering. He took the male goat for the people’s sin offering, slaughtered it, and offered it for sin like the first one.”*

- **“Like the first one”** means Aaron followed the same ritual as for his own sin offering (vv. 8–11). The people’s sin offering mirrored the priest’s. Guzik emphasizes the principle: Aaron “must receive God’s atoning sacrifice first. It was only then that he could properly bring the people’s offering.” (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-9/)

---

### v. 16 — *“He presented the burnt offering and offered it according to the ordinance.”*

- **“According to the ordinance”** (or “prescribed manner”) — Aaron followed the regulations laid down in Leviticus 1 for the burnt offering. This was done “by the book,” an important precedent at the inauguration of the sacrificial system. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-9/)

---

### v. 17 — *“Next he presented the grain offering, took a handful of it, and burned it on the altar in addition to the morning’s burnt offering.”*

- **“In addition to the morning’s burnt offering.”** This reveals that the regular daily morning sacrifice (Ex 29:38–42) was already being offered, presumably by Moses until now. The special offerings of this inaugural day were supplementary to, not a replacement for, the daily regular offerings. (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/expositors/leviticus/9.htm)
- **The “handful” (memorial portion)** — following Leviticus 2:2, only a memorial portion was burned; the rest belonged to the priests (Lev 10:12). (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/pfc/leviticus-9.html)

---

### vv. 18–21 — *The people’s peace offering*

- **v. 18 — Ox and ram slaughtered; blood sprinkled.** Gill: the peace offering was so the people “might feast, rejoice, and be glad that atonement was made for their sins, and their gifts and sacrifices accepted of God, see Romans 5:11.” (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/leviticus/9-18.htm)
- **vv. 19–20 — Fat portions laid on the breasts.** The fat tail, the fat covering the entrails, the kidneys, and lobe of the liver were laid on the breasts. The fat was God’s portion and was burned. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-9/)
- **v. 21 — Wave offering: breasts and right thigh.** Aaron waved the breasts and right thigh before the LORD “as Moses had commanded.” Peake’s Commentary notes a textual issue: the thigh being waved (rather than “heaved”) here may be a later gloss from Lev 7:30, since in Lev 8 the thigh is not mentioned, and in Lev 10:14 the traditional distinction (breast waved, thigh heaved) is preserved. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/pfc/leviticus-9.html)

---

### v. 22 — *“Aaron lifted up his hands toward the people and blessed them. And having made the sin offering, the burnt offering, and the peace offering, he stepped down.”*

- **The priestly blessing.** The Expositor’s Bible Commentary presumes Aaron used the form prescribed in Numbers 6:24–27: “The LORD bless thee, and keep thee…”. The Chaldee Version reports the blessing as: “May the Word of Jehovah accept your sacrifice with favour, and remit and pardon your sins.” (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-9/ ; https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/expositors/leviticus/9.htm)
- **Blessing follows sacrifice.** Guzik: “It may also be of significance that blessing follows the sacrifices made on behalf of the people. This illustrates the New Testament truth that every spiritual blessing comes to the Christian as a result of the sacrifice of Jesus Christ upon the cross.” (Rooker, cited by Guzik) (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-9/)
- **Aaron lifted his hands** — a gesture still used in many Christian traditions for blessing. The Expositor’s Bible notes the parallel: Jesus “lifted up His hands, and blessed them” (Luke 24:50) before ascending. (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/expositors/leviticus/9.htm)
- **Matthew Henry:** “Aaron could but crave a blessing, God alone can command it.” (https://www.preceptaustin.org/leviticus_9_commentary)

---

### v. 23 — *“Moses and Aaron then entered the Tent of Meeting. When they came out, they blessed the people, and the glory of the LORD appeared to all the people.”*

- **The double benediction.** First Aaron alone blessed (v. 22), then Moses and Aaron together entered the tabernacle, came out, and blessed the people again. The Expositor’s Bible Commentary sees this as significant: Aaron’s outer-court work was finished; now he must be inducted into the Holy Place work (incense, lamps, showbread), which typifies Christ’s heavenly intercession after His earthly sacrifice. (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/expositors/leviticus/9.htm)
- **G. Campbell Morgan:** “The servants of God, whether prophets or priests, have no power to bless men save as they receive it in direct communion with God. Before we can go out and bless the people, we must go in to the Place of Meeting with God… Forgetfulness of this is the secret of much futility in Christian work.” (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-9/)
- **“The glory of the LORD appeared.”** This was probably a visible, extraordinary brightness from the pillar of cloud — or an overwhelming sense of God’s presence. Ellicott: “God manifested himself in the more luminous appearance of the cloudy pillar… visible in greater effulgence to all the people.” Peake’s Commentary: the glory, naturally connected with fire, was ordinarily shrouded by cloud from the people during the day. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/leviticus-9.html ; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/pfc/leviticus-9.html)

---

### v. 24 — *“Fire came out from the presence of the LORD and consumed the burnt offering and the fat portions on the altar. And when all the people saw it, they shouted for joy and fell facedown.”*

- **The nature of the miracle.** Keil (cited at StudyLight.org): the miracle was not that fire ignited the sacrifices (they were already burning), but that “the sacrifices, which were already on fire, were SUDDENLY consumed.” Constable agrees: “In this way God manifested His satisfaction with this first sacrifice that the newly consecrated priests offered.” Benson: “This fire now given was to be carefully kept, and not suffered to go out (Lev 6:13), and therefore was carried in a peculiar vessel in their journeys.” (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/leviticus/9-24.html ; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/leviticus-9.html ; https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/benson/leviticus/9.htm)
- **Fire = divine acceptance.** Gill explains the two-fold significance: (1) God’s wrath, which should have consumed the people, fastened on the sacrifice instead — signifying acceptance of the atonement; (2) God “entering into covenant and communion with them: they ate their part of the sacrifice, and the fire of the Lord ate up his part” (cf. Rev 3:20). (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/leviticus/9-24.html)
- **Six biblical examples of fire from heaven accepting a sacrifice:** Aaron (Lev 9:24), Gideon (Jdg 6:21), Manoah (Jdg 13:19–23), David (1 Chr 21:26), Solomon (2 Chr 7:1), Elijah (1 Kgs 18:38). (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-9/)
- **The source of the fire.** Ellicott: “from the luminous cloud flashes of fire.” Some think it was lightning; Josephus (cited by Clarke) thought the sacrifices ignited spontaneously from the altar itself. The key point: it was unmistakably from God, not trickery — it was “publicly evident to the entire people of Israel.” (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-9/)
- **“They shouted for joy and fell facedown.”** The Hebrew *ranan* means to shout for joy — this is the first occurrence of a word for “joy” in the Bible. “Fell on their faces” implies the face touched the ground, “an indication of the most profound and deepest respect before a superior.” (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-9/ ; https://www.studylight.org/commentary/leviticus/9-24.html)
- **Typology of the Spirit.** Benson: “Thus the Spirit descended in fire upon the apostles, so ratifying their commission, as this did that of the priests. And the descent of this holy fire into our souls, to kindle in them devout affections… is a certain token of God’s gracious acceptance.” Matthew Henry adds: “Hereby we know that we dwell in God, and God in us, because he hath thus given us of his Spirit, 1 John 4:13.” (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/benson/leviticus/9.htm ; https://www.preceptaustin.org/leviticus_9_commentary)

---

## Where Protestant Traditions Differ (or Emphasise Distinctively)

### Reformed / Presbyterian

The Expositor’s Bible Commentary (from a broadly Reformed perspective) draws out the **ordo salutis** (order of salvation) from the progression of offerings: sin offering (justification, expiation), then burnt offering (sanctification, full consecration), then peace offering (fellowship with God). This order is presented as “an invariable law” of the spiritual life — the believer first apprehends Christ as Sin Offering (propitiation), then as Burnt Offering (righteousness through full consecration), and finally as Peace Offering (life and fellowship). The commentary explicitly links this to Romans 6–7 and 2 Corinthians 5:13–15. (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/expositors/leviticus/9.htm)

### Baptist

- **Gill (older Baptist):** Emphasises the imperfection of the Levitical priesthood (“a man cannot atone for another until he is pure from all sin”) and its fulfilment in Christ alone, citing Hebrews 7:27. He reads the fire typologically as both God’s wrath consumed on the sacrifice and God’s covenant fellowship with His people. (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/leviticus/9.htm)
- **Garner-Howes Baptist Commentary:** Stresses the public nature of the fire as divine approval and the people’s awe and prostration as the model of worship. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/leviticus-9.html)

### Methodist / Wesleyan

- **Benson Commentary:** Reads the fire as a token of God’s approval of the priesthood and the sacrifices, emphasising the moral/spiritual application: “the descent of this holy fire into our souls, to kindle in them devout affections, and such a holy zeal as burns up all unholiness, is a certain token of God’s gracious acceptance.” This reflects the Wesleyan emphasis on sanctification and holy living. (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/benson/leviticus/9.htm)
- **Matthew Henry** (widely used across traditions): “Aaron could but crave a blessing, God alone can command it.” Emphasises that our best services still need washing in Christ’s blood. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/leviticus_9_commentary)

### Pentecostal / Charismatic

- **David Guzik (Enduring Word):** Though broadly evangelical, his Pentecostal emphasis appears in the application of the fire: “Fire was often associated with God’s presence and work… John the Baptist promised Jesus would come with a baptism of the Holy Spirit and with fire (Matthew 3:11). The Holy Spirit manifested His presence on the day of Pentecost by tongues of fire (Acts 2:3).” Guzik draws a strong line from the Levitical fire to the Day of Pentecost, making this a pattern for Spirit-empowered worship today. He also emphasises the public, undeniable nature of the fire — “This was, beyond any doubt, God’s fire and not from man” — a theme resonant in Pentecostal/charismatic expectation of manifest divine presence. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-9/)

### Anglican

- **Ellicott’s Commentary:** Offers careful philological and historical notes (e.g., explaining the “calf, the son of a bull” as a technical term for a two-year-old). Notes the ancient tradition connecting the bull-calf to the golden calf incident. Highlights the double benediction and the Christological parallel of Aaron blessing then disappearing into the tabernacle (cf. Luke 24:50–51). (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/leviticus-9.html)

---

## Other Views

### Modern Scholarship

- **Peake’s Commentary (early 20th c. critical scholarship):** Notes textual and source-critical issues. Observes that “elders” (v. 1) are “mentioned nowhere else in P save Leviticus 4:15.” Asks why no guilt offering is mentioned (cf. Lev 5:17). Suggests the right thigh being “waved” (v. 21) may be a gloss added from Lev 7:30, since in Lev 8 the thigh is not mentioned and in Lev 10:14 the distinction of waving vs. heaving is preserved. Also suggests the author may have “neglected” the fact that the offerings were already burning before the fire came. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/pfc/leviticus-9.html)
- **NET Bible notes and Bible Odyssey** (bibleodyssey.org, netbible.org) — not available in the fetched sources. Unable to retrieve these within search limits.

### Catholic and Orthodox Readings

- Unable to retrieve pages from newadvent.org, catholic.com, or oca.org within search limits. The Haydock Catholic Commentary (typically on studylight.org) was not fetched. The Expositor’s Bible Commentary (Protestant but with broad historical awareness) notes the Chaldee/Targum tradition and rabbinical interpretations throughout, which informs both Catholic and Orthodox typological reading.

### Debated Popular Modern Teaching

- No specific prosperity, Word of Faith, or hyper-grace teaching on Leviticus 9 was found in the searched sources. However, the chapter is sometimes cited in charismatic circles regarding “the fire of God.” Guzik’s application — that “the priests were there, the offering was there… but it was all incomplete without the fire from God” — can be used (and sometimes is) to teach that correct doctrine and ritual are insufficient without a tangible manifestation of divine presence, a theme popular in Pentecostal and revivalist preaching. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-9/)

---

### Summary of the Sacrificial Progression (Morgan)

G. Campbell Morgan summarises the theological progression: “Carefully observe this order. Sin put away, life and work devoted, communion made possible; then the priestly blessing, speaking of acceptance, followed by a second blessing, which declared the divine satisfaction as it was accompanied by the manifestation of glory, and so finally the full worship of the people.” (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-9/)
